## Lecture 2: Memory Evolution — Memory Hierarchy and SOTA

Prof. Kai Chen

<!-- page: 2 -->

## Syllabus and Readings

## Key Question

How to design memory systems to fully utilize modern CPUs/GPUs, especially in the AI era?

## Today's Path

[Review] Von Neumann Architecture.

[Core] Memory wall: performance is limited by data supply.

[Core] CPU vs GPU memory subsystem.

[Concept] Memory Technology Evolution.

## CPU Memory Hierarchy

## Memory Hierarchy: Taking Advantage of Locality

For frequent data: use fast but expensive and small memory (e.g., cache)

For not frequent data: use slow but cheap and large memory (e.g., main memory, disk)

## CPU Memory Hierarchy

### Hit or Miss of Caches: Benefit vs. Penalty

Hit: The requested memory block is found in the current cache level, with a valid tag match.

Hit Rate: Hits / Total Accesses

Cache Read/Write: Find the data on cache and then perform read/write Miss: The requested memory block is not present in the current cache level, so it must be retrieved from the next lower level.



Miss Rate: 1 - Hit Rate

Miss Penalty: The additional time required to service a miss

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_243_858_1741_1343.jpg" alt="Image" width="74%" /></div>

<!-- page: 26 -->

Access Time: Latency for the memory to handle one access Transfer Time: Latency to transfer data block to higher level Miss penalty = access time + data size / bandwidth

## CPU Memory Hierarchy

## Average Memory Access Time (AMAT)

AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate  $ \times $ Miss penalty

## Miss Penalty: time to fetch a block from lower memory level

A cache helps when common hits remain fast and sufficiently few accesses pay the miss penalty.

## CPU Memory Hierarchy

### DRAM Behind Cache: SRAM vs. DRAM

## SRAM --- Store data via stable transistor circuit

Requires low power to retain bit (423mV for 45nm)

Requires 6 transistors/bit --- expansive

Usage: Caches, register files

## DRAM --- Store date via tiny capacitors (bit is represented as charged and discharged)

One transistor/bit --- cheap

Must be re-written after being read

Must also be periodically refreshed

Each row can be refreshed simultaneously

Address lines are multiplexed:

Upper half of address: row access strobe (RAS)

Lower half of address: column access strobe (CAS)

Usage: DDR / GDDR / HBM

## CPU Memory Hierarchy

## DRAM Behind Cache: Why DRAM is Slow?

## Weak storage signal

DRAM stores bits as tiny capacitor charges, producing only a small voltage difference on long bitlines.

## Sensing takes time

The sense amplifier must detect and amplify a very small voltage change into a full 0/1 value.

## Destructive read

Reading a DRAM cell disturbs its stored charge, so the data must be restored after every row activation.

## Large dense arrays

DRAM prioritizes capacity and cost per bit, so rows/bitlines are long and have higher RC delay.

Solution: Multi-Bank, Multi-Rank DRAM

## GPU Memory Hierarchy

## Access Memory: Coalescing Packs Nearby Addresses into Fewer Transactions

## aligned + CONTIGUOUS

Minimum transactions

Transactions: 1-few

## MISALIGNED

Crosses an extra boundary

Transactions: few + 1

## STRIDED

Touches many segments

Transactions: many

Coalescing is evaluated per warp instruction and depends on access width, alignment, cache-sector size, and architecture.

Coalescing is evaluated for one warp memory instruction. Aligned, contiguous addresses touch fewer segments.

Misalignment can cross extra boundaries. Strided accesses can touch many more segments.

## SOTA Memory Technologies

## Tiered Memory Management Decides What Stays in HBM

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_262_335_1716_1007.jpg" alt="Image" width="72%" /></div>


Migration is useful only when future reuse repays transfer cost. Granularity, prediction accuracy, and placement overhead determine the result.

Keep hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM. Place large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier.

Promotion helps only when future reuse saves more than the transfer and bookkeeping cost.
